title: What We Learned About AI and Education in 2023
author: Nick Potkalitsky
summary: Potkalitsky's year-end review takes stock of the first year after ChatGPT's launch and argues that education is moving from disruption toward a phase of experimentation and integration, as it did with the calculator and the internet. He surveys policy and privacy questions (FERPA, school AI-use policies), AI literacy gaps among teachers, model and interface developments, AI tutoring such as Khanmigo, writing instruction, assessment, and bias and accessibility research. His stance is openly pro-integration: he regards bans and AI detectors as hasty and counterproductive and wants evidence-based curricula built through collaborative classroom experimentation. The piece moves from description to a set of recommendations for AI-responsive educators, including trust-based classroom relationships, honest self-assessment of AI literacy, and modelling AI as editor and thought-partner. Reposted from a guest spot at AI Supremacy, it is useful as a dated snapshot of the early-2024 school AI debate, though much of the survey is brief and relies on other writers' work.
points: Potkalitsky frames AI as the latest technology to pass through a cycle of disruption, experimentation, and normalization, and argues schools are still stuck at disruption.
He urges schools to write AI-use policies with stated rationales and to ask concrete data-privacy questions (age limits, what companies store) before assigning student LLM use.
On tutoring, he sides with Dan Meyer's view that tutoring is mostly motivational, so tools like Khanmigo are unlikely to make teachers replaceable.
For assessment he endorses a 'two-lane' model of supervised assessment of learning plus unsupervised assessment for learning that invites responsible AI engagement.
His closing recommendations favour slow, trust-based, collaboratively tested adoption over AI detectors and bans.
quotes: Yet, in each instance, a resilient group of teachers, administrators, researchers, and policymakers advocated for experimentation in the utilization, implementation, and integration of these tools and resources into schools and classrooms.
Meanwhile, students are eager for more than just a “give-it-a-try” methodology. They seek a rigorous, evidence-based curriculum that prepares them for the realities of work in college and beyond.

In the absence of strong guidance from federal or state authorities, educational institutions bear the great responsibility of providing a safety net for both educators and students using these rapidly advancing products.

In high school settings, studies suggest that 10-20% of students use AI to assist with the majority of their writing assignments. These figures should be a wake-up call for educators who underestimate AI's presence or overestimate the efficacy of AI detectors.

This includes ‘assessment of learning,’ supervised assessments authenticating mastery of specific knowledge and skills, and ‘assessment for learning,’ unsupervised assessments encouraging responsible AI engagement. This “two-lane” approach transforms quizzes, tests, and exams from mere memorization exercises into knowledge-constituting experiences.
In the realm of AI in education, hastily adopted solutions, such as AI detectors or bans, often miss the mark. Emphasizing slow, deliberate, and experimental change is crucial.

The teacher-student relationship should be anchored in trust, honesty, and accountability, especially in light of the challenges posed by AI. Educators must engage students as informed partners in the learning process, respecting their individuality and agency.
